newsitem.title: ITALY: Scope for more Italy monetary easing expected - IMF.
newsitem.headline: Scope for more Italy monetary easing expected - IMF.

text.p: Italian interest rates should fall further, but the timing of any rate cut depended on approval of the 1997 budget and on major wage settlements currently under review, the International Monetary Fund said in a report.

"The presence of a large output gap, continued disinflation, and favourable exchange market conditions should provide scope for further cuts in official interest rates," the IMF said in a provisional survey following a visit by IMF experts.
The official discount rate currently stands at 7.5 percent compared with nine percent at the start of the year.

"The desirable scenario for 1997 is one in which monetary policy plays a supporting role in cushioning the short-term contractionary effect of fiscal tightening without taking risks on inflation," the IMF said.

But before the Bank of Italy cut rates, it would have to wait until the government's 1997 austerity budget was approved by parliament. Under Italian law, the package has to be passed by both houses of parliament before the end of the year.
The IMF said monetary easing also depended on a "satisfactory outcome" to wage negotiations currently going on in the metalworkers' and engineering sector.

Trades' unions representing some 1.7 million workers in the sector, which accounts for about 40 percent of total manufacturing output in Italy, are locked in dispute with management over pay increases for the 1996-1998 period.
Unions want full compensation for an overshoot in inflation in the past contract period and have already called two one-day strikes to press home their demands.
Management say they cannot afford the wage claim and received backing in the IMF report.

"While some degree of real wage catch-up has been included in most contracts concluded to date without generating inflationary pressures, a full catch-up...would be at odds with the spirit of the 1993 agreement," the IMF said.
Under the terms of a landmark 1993 accord, automatic index-linked pay increases were scrapped.
The government said earlier on Monday that all the elements were in place for a deal in the long-running dispute. -- Rome newsroom +396 6782501
